units.title: Sentences
units.blurb: A sentence tells a whole idea. It starts with a capital letter and ends with a period, a question mark or an exclamation point.

units.title: Naming Words and Action Words
units.blurb: Nouns name people, places, animals and things; verbs tell what they do, and when.

units.title: Describing Words
units.blurb: Adjectives and sense words paint a picture, and a plain sentence can grow with them.

units.title: Capital Letters
units.blurb: The word I, names of people and pets, days, months, holidays and places all begin with capitals.

units.title: Spelling Patterns
units.blurb: Short vowels, letter pairs like sh and ch, the silent e, vowel teams, word endings, and the tricky words to know by heart.

units.title: Joining Ideas
units.blurb: And, but, because and so join ideas; commas keep a list neat.

units.title: Writing About a Picture
units.blurb: Tell who, what and where, match the picture, and stay on one topic.

units.title: Letters and Notes
units.blurb: The parts of a friendly letter, greetings and closings, and a thank-you note worth sending.

units.title: Telling a Story
units.blurb: Beginning, middle and end, time words, characters and setting, a problem and a fix, how-to steps, and an opinion with a reason.

units.title: Checking Your Writing
units.blurb: Read it back and fix it: capitals, end marks, spaces and spelling.

topics.title: What Is a Sentence?
topics.short: A sentence tells a whole idea: it names who or what, and tells what happens.
topics.trouble: Children write part of an idea, like “The big dog.” or “Ran to the park.”, and call it a sentence because it has a capital letter and a period. Ask: who or what? What happens?

topics.title: Words in the Right Order
topics.short: The words of a sentence go in an order that makes sense: usually who or what first, then what happens.
topics.trouble: Children write words in the order they think of them (“Ball the kicked Sam.”) and don’t read the sentence back aloud to hear whether it makes sense.

topics.title: Start with a Capital Letter
topics.short: The first word of every sentence begins with a capital letter.
topics.trouble: Children forget the capital at the start of the second or third sentence, or sprinkle capital letters in the middle of words and sentences.

topics.title: Telling Sentences
topics.short: A telling sentence tells something. It ends with a period.
topics.trouble: Children put a period at the end of every line of writing instead of at the end of each idea, or leave the period off the last sentence.

topics.title: Asking Sentences
topics.short: An asking sentence asks something. It ends with a question mark.
topics.trouble: Children put a question mark after a telling sentence that has a question word in it (“I know where the ball is?”), or a period after a real question.

topics.title: Exclamations
topics.short: An exclamation shows strong feeling, like surprise, joy or fear. It ends with an exclamation point.
topics.trouble: Children put exclamation points on every sentence, or several in a row (“!!!”). One exclamation point, saved for strong feeling, works best.

topics.title: Bossy Sentences
topics.short: A command tells someone to do something: “Please shut the door.” It usually ends with a period.
topics.trouble: Children think a command is not a sentence because nobody is named. The person you are talking to is the one who does it.

topics.title: Which End Mark?
topics.short: Read the whole sentence. Does it tell, ask or show strong feeling? Then choose the period, question mark or exclamation point.
topics.trouble: Children choose the mark from the first word alone. “What a big cake!” starts like a question but shows surprise, so it is an exclamation.

topics.title: Nouns: Naming Words
topics.short: A noun names a person, a place, an animal or a thing: Grandma, park, puppy, cup.
topics.trouble: Children count only things they can touch, and miss nouns for people and places like teacher, kitchen and city.

topics.title: One and More Than One
topics.short: Add -s to most nouns to mean more than one: cats. Add -es after s, x, sh, ch and z: buses, boxes, dishes.
topics.trouble: Children write boxs and dishs, or add -s to nouns that change in their own way (mouses, foots, childs).

topics.title: Verbs: Action Words
topics.short: A verb tells what someone or something does: run, eat, sing, sleep, think.
topics.trouble: Children pick the person or thing instead of the action, and miss quiet verbs that are not big movements, like sleep, wish and know.

topics.title: Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow
topics.short: Verbs show when something happens: yesterday I walked, today I walk, tomorrow I will walk.
topics.trouble: Children add -ed to every verb, even ones that change another way (runned, goed), and mix times in one story.

topics.title: Is, Are, Was and Were
topics.short: Use is and was with one; use are and were with more than one, and with you. A verb matches its noun: he hops, we hop.
topics.trouble: Many people say “we was” or “they is” in everyday talk. Written standard English uses we were and they are, so writing needs the matching verb.

topics.title: He, She, It and They
topics.short: Pronouns like I, he, she, it, we and they take the place of nouns, so we don’t say the same name again and again.
topics.trouble: Children start sentences with “Me and him…”. In writing, the one who does the action is he, she, I or they: “He and I played.”

topics.title: Describing Words
topics.short: Adjectives describe nouns: what color, what size, what shape, how many, and how something looks, sounds or feels.
topics.trouble: Children pick the noun instead of the word that describes it, or use only a few tired words like nice, good and big.

topics.title: Words for the Five Senses
topics.short: Sense words tell how something looks, sounds, smells, tastes and feels: shiny, crunchy, sweet, soft, loud.
topics.trouble: Children describe only how things look and forget the sounds, smells, tastes and feelings that make writing come alive.

topics.title: Make a Sentence Grow
topics.short: Add describing words and where or when words to a plain sentence: “The dog ran.” → “The little brown dog ran to the lake.”
topics.trouble: Children add details that don’t match the picture, or add so many that the sentence runs on and on.

topics.title: Capital I
topics.short: When you write about yourself, the word I is always a capital letter.
topics.trouble: Children write a small i in the middle of a sentence (“Mom and i baked bread.”).

topics.title: Names of People and Pets
topics.short: Names of people and pets begin with capital letters: Sam, Grandma Rose, Dr. Bell, Biscuit.
topics.trouble: Children capitalize every noun (Dog, Ball) or forget the capital on a pet’s name. Grandma is a name in “Hi, Grandma!” but not in “my grandma.”

topics.title: Days, Months and Holidays
topics.short: Days of the week, months and holidays begin with capital letters: Monday, May, Thanksgiving. Seasons do not: spring, summer.
topics.trouble: Children capitalize the seasons (Summer), or forget the capital on the days and months.

topics.title: Names of Places
topics.short: The name of one special place begins with capitals: Oak Street, Lincoln Park, Texas, the Pacific Ocean.
topics.trouble: Children capitalize any word for a place (“the Park”) instead of only a place’s own name (“Lincoln Park”).

topics.title: Short Vowel Words
topics.short: In words like cat, bed, pig, hot and bug, one vowel between two consonants usually makes its short sound.
topics.trouble: Children mix up short e and short i (pen and pin), or leave the vowel out (ct for cat).

topics.title: Sh, Ch, Th, Wh and Ck
topics.short: Two letters can spell one sound: ship, chip, thin, when, and duck at the end of a short word.
topics.trouble: Children write one letter for the sound (sip for ship, cin for chin), or use ck at the start of a word (ckat).

topics.title: The Silent E
topics.short: An e at the end of a short word makes the vowel say its name: cap → cape, kit → kite, hop → hope.
topics.trouble: Children leave off the final e (kit for kite), or add one to a short-vowel word (hate for hat).

topics.title: Vowel Teams
topics.short: Two letters together often spell one long vowel sound: rain, play, feet, beach, boat, snow.
topics.trouble: Several teams spell the same sound (rain and play; feet and beach), so children pick the wrong one. Reading a lot helps you remember which team a word uses.

topics.title: Adding -s, -ed and -ing
topics.short: Add endings to show more than one or when: jumps, jumped, jumping. In short words like hop, double the last letter: hopped, hopping.
topics.trouble: Children forget to double the letter (hoping when they mean hopping), or keep a silent e before -ing (hopeing).

topics.title: Tricky Words to Know by Heart
topics.short: Some common words don’t follow the usual patterns: said, was, of, they, could, because, friend. Learn them by heart.
topics.trouble: Children spell these words the way they sound (sed, wuz, uv, thay, becuz).

topics.title: Joining with And
topics.short: Use and to join two short sentences that go together: “I have a cat, and she is gray.”
topics.trouble: Children join every sentence with and (“and then… and then… and then…”), so the writing becomes one long string.

topics.title: Joining with But
topics.short: Use but to join two ideas that are different, or when the second one is a surprise: “I like snow, but my dog does not.”
topics.trouble: Children use but when the two ideas agree (“I like dogs, but I have a dog.”).

topics.title: Because and So
topics.short: Because gives a reason. So tells what happened as a result: “I was cold, so I put on a coat.”
topics.trouble: Children swap the reason and the result: “I was hungry because I ate lunch.” The reason comes right after because.

topics.title: Commas in a List
topics.short: Put commas between three or more things in a list: “We packed apples, grapes, and cheese.”
topics.trouble: Children put a comma after every word, or between just two things joined by and. Some writers leave out the comma before and; both ways are used.

topics.title: Who, What and Where
topics.short: A good sentence about a picture tells who is in it, what they are doing, and where.
topics.trouble: Children list things in the picture (“A dog. A ball. A tree.”) instead of telling what is happening.

topics.title: Does It Match the Picture?
topics.short: Choose the sentence that tells what the picture really shows.
topics.trouble: Children pick a sentence that sounds nice but adds things that are not in the picture.

topics.title: Stay on Topic
topics.short: All the sentences about one picture or one idea should be about that idea.
topics.trouble: Children add a sentence about something else in the middle (“I like pizza.” in sentences about a dog).

topics.title: Tell What It Is About
topics.short: Start with a sentence that names your topic, give some facts, and finish with a sentence that wraps up.
topics.trouble: Children jump straight into details and never say what the writing is about, or stop without an ending sentence.

topics.title: The Parts of a Friendly Letter
topics.short: A friendly letter has a date, a greeting, a body, a closing and a signature.
topics.trouble: Children forget the greeting or the signature, or write the closing at the top.

topics.title: Greetings and Closings
topics.short: Start with a greeting like “Dear Grandma,” and end with a closing like “Love,” each with a comma.
topics.trouble: Children leave out the comma after the greeting or closing, or capitalize every word of the closing (“Your Friend,”).

topics.title: A Thank-You Note
topics.short: Thank the person, say what you liked about the gift or the kind thing they did, and sign your name.
topics.trouble: Children write only “Thanks for the gift.” without naming the gift or saying one thing about it.

topics.title: Beginning, Middle and End
topics.short: A story has a beginning (who and where), a middle (what happens) and an end (how it works out).
topics.trouble: Children stop in the middle (“…and then I woke up.”) without an ending that wraps the story up.

topics.title: First, Next, Then, Last
topics.short: Time words like first, next, then, after that and last help a reader follow the order.
topics.trouble: Children use “and then” for every step, or use last before the last step.

topics.title: Characters and Setting
topics.short: The characters are who the story is about. The setting is where and when it happens.
topics.trouble: Children call the place a character, or forget to tell where and when the story happens.

topics.title: A Problem and a Fix
topics.short: Many stories have a problem in the middle and a fix at the end.
topics.trouble: Children solve the problem right away, so the story has no middle.

topics.title: How-To Writing
topics.short: Tell how to do something, with every step in order, so a reader could follow it.
topics.trouble: Children skip steps that seem obvious to them, like getting the bread out before spreading the jam.

topics.title: I Think, Because
topics.short: An opinion says what you think and gives a reason: “I think dogs are the best pets because they love to play.”
topics.trouble: Children give an opinion with no reason, or give a fact (“Dogs have four legs.”) when asked for an opinion.

topics.title: Check Your Writing
topics.short: Read your writing back. Check capital letters, spaces between words, end marks, and words spelled the best you can.
topics.trouble: Children say “I’m done” without reading the writing back. Reading it aloud catches most mistakes.

topics.title: Fix the Sentence
topics.short: Find and fix every mistake in a sentence: a missing capital, a missing end mark, a wrong word.
topics.trouble: Children fix one mistake and stop. A sentence can have more than one.
